text: Choosing a governance model answers who can change the platform. This lesson answers a different question: once you're actually rolling a new capability out across several departments with genuinely different needs, in what order, and what exactly gets built once versus built per department?

Launching a new capability everywhere at once multiplies every unknown by the number of departments involved — if the design has a flaw, every department discovers it simultaneously, with none yet convinced it actually works. The real alternative is a single pilot department, chosen for the clearest, most contained use case, not the biggest or most important one. A clean pilot win builds real, demonstrated confidence that makes the harder departments willing to adopt without a fight, instead of fighting the rollout from day one because the first thing they saw was a struggle.

Every rollout forces the same line Chapter 2's scoped-application work raised. The base intake form, the core data model, the workflow engine, notifications — anything every department needs in the same shape belongs in a shared scoped application, maintained once. Approval routing, department-unique fields, department-level reporting — anything genuinely different per department belongs in an extension built on that shared base, not a fork of it. Forcing one into the other is expensive either way.

A real rollout builds the shared base and the pilot's own extension together, launches, and gathers actual usage friction instead of hypothetical design-review concerns. Fixes go into the shared base, so every later department benefits immediately, instead of each department rediscovering and re-fixing the same problem on its own schedule. The remaining departments get sequenced roughly by complexity, each adding only its own extension on top of a base the pilot already proved out in real use.

Sequencing and the shared-versus-specific line are architecture decisions. Lesson 27 covers the other side of making a rollout actually happen: translating those decisions for executive stakeholders who hold the budget, and don't share your technical vocabulary.
